BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) -- Amid high emotions and tight security, thousands lined the streets of Beirut Friday to honor Antoine Ghanem, the anti-Syrian Lebanese MP killed in a powerful bomb blast along with four others. Amin Gemayel (R), Phalange party head, carries the coffin of assassinated deputy Antoine Ghamen. Against an atmosphere of intense political and patriotic fervor, the flag-draped coffins of the politician and two bodyguards also killed in Wednesday's rush hour blast made its way through the city's Christian district to the Sacred Heart church on what the government had declared as a day of national mourning. The procession was accompanied by thousands waving flags, as well as a brass band playing the anthem of Ghanem's Phalange Party, The Associated Press reported . TV pictures showed distraught mourners crowding and reaching out to the coffins as they were carried aloft. Several people were seen to collapse and had to be carried away. Mourners also carried photographs, threw rose petals and unfurled banners, some of which read "We Won't Kneel," AP said. The coffins were greeted at the Christian Maronite church with applause from the gathered mourners, the agency said, including majority leaders and the Lebanese cabinet as well as Ghanem's family and friends. Ghanem was later buried in the city's Christian district. Ghanem's death is the latest in a series of attacks targeting prominent anti-Syrian figures, with the most notorious being the February 2005 assassination in Beirut of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri, which sparked widespread protests that led to the ouster of Syrian forces from Lebanon. Hariri also died in a massive explosion. The incident threatens to cast the country into political uncertainty ahead of a key presidential vote in a tightly divided parliament, almost evenly split between anti- and pro-Syrian camps.  Watch how Ghanem's death disrupts Lebanese politics » . CNN's Beirut bureau chief Brent Sadler said that many Lebanese now feared for the future, especially given other events in the region including the conflict between Palestinians and Israelis, recent political differences in Iraq and Iran's bid to become a super power. "There continues to be among a great deal of people here a sense of foreboding that perhaps the worst is yet to come," he said. U.S. President George W. Bush, in a written statement, joined other world leaders in condemning the "horrific assassination." "Since October 2004, there has been a tragic pattern of political assassinations and attempted assassinations designed to silence those Lebanese who courageously defend their vision of an independent and democratic Lebanon," Bush said Wednesday. Also in a written statement, a spokesperson for Ban Ki-moon said the U.N. secretary-general "condemns in the strongest terms this terrorist attack." "The secretary general urges all Lebanese to exercise utmost calm and restraint at this very critical time and to allow judicial procedures to take their course," the spokesperson said. Bush's statement added: "The United States opposes any attempts to intimidate the Lebanese people as they seek to exercise their democratic right to select a president without foreign interference. We will continue to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the Lebanese people as they resist attempts by the Syrian and Iranian regimes and their allies to destabilize Lebanon and undermine its sovereignty." The U.S. Embassy in Beirut issued a statement saying: "It is not a coincidence that these attacks target those figures who have been working to secure Lebanon's independence from renewed Syrian hegemony. We note with concern that many Lebanese politicians allied with Syria have in fact warned that murder and violence would be the results of any effort to exercise genuine parliamentary democracy." And U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, in a written statement, said: "The bombing that claimed these lives was another act in a campaign of terror by those who want to turn back the clock on Lebanon's hard-won democratic gains." "The world should speak with one voice in calling for an end to violence in Lebanon intended to subvert democratic processes in that country," Rice said. "Lebanese elections, scheduled to begin in just days, must proceed, in accordance with the Constitution, without threats of foreign interference and the violence that accompanies such obstruction." **Mourners Gather in Beirut for Funeral of Slain Anti-Syrian MP Antoine Ghanem**

**BEIRUT, Lebanon** — Thousands of angry and grieving mourners filled the streets of Beirut on Friday for the funeral of assassinated lawmaker Antoine Ghanem, turning the solemn service into a defiant rally against political violence just days before a crucial presidential election.

Ghanem, a 64-year-old Christian MP and member of the anti-Syrian Kataeb (Phalange) Party, was killed on Wednesday alongside two bodyguards and two civilians when a powerful car bomb tore through his vehicle in the suburban Beirut district of Sin el-Fil. 

His coffin, draped in the Lebanese national flag and the green cedar banner of the Kataeb Party, was carried on the shoulders of weeping supporters through his home district of Furn el-Chebbak toward the Sacred Heart Church. Mourners threw rice and white rose petals from balconies as the procession passed, while crowd members chanted slogans demanding an end to assassinations and condemning Syrian influence in Lebanon.

Ghanem was the eighth prominent anti-Syrian figure—and the fourth governing coalition lawmaker—to be assassinated in Lebanon since the February 2005 murder of former Prime Minister Rafic Hariri. 

The funeral was attended by prominent figures of the ruling "March 14" coalition, including former President Amin Gemayel, whose own son, Industry Minister Pierre Gemayel, was assassinated in a similar fashion late last year. 

Addressing the congregation, an emotional Gemayel paid tribute to Ghanem while issuing a stark warning about the threats facing Lebanese independence. 

"Antoine Ghanem died so that Lebanon could live," Gemayel said. "They are trying to liquidate our majority, to assassinate our democracy. But we will not bow down, and we will not allow them to destroy our republic."

Security was exceptionally tight across the capital, with army troops, armored personnel carriers, and armed police deployed along major intersections. Tensions in the country have reached a fever pitch, as Ghanem’s death reduced the Western-backed ruling coalition’s slim majority in parliament ahead of a vital legislative vote scheduled for next week to elect a new president.

Ghanem had returned to Lebanon only two days prior to his assassination, having spent several months in self-imposed exile in Europe out of fear for his life. Many majority lawmakers have been living in high-security hotels in Beirut, surrounded by heavy guards, to protect the governing bloc's fragile parliamentary majority.

Leaders of the March 14 alliance have openly pointed the finger at Damascus, accusing the Syrian regime of carrying out a targeted campaign of political assassinations to undermine Lebanese sovereignty and block the election of an anti-Syrian president to succeed outgoing President Emile Lahoud.

Syria has strongly denied any involvement in the bombing, issuing a statement condemning the attack as an attempt to derail efforts at Lebanese national reconciliation.

As the funeral service concluded, Ghanem’s body was taken to his family tomb for burial. The atmosphere in Beirut remained heavy with apprehension, as the political deadlock between the U.S.-backed majority and the Hezbollah-led opposition threatens to plunge the country into a deeper constitutional crisis.

**CNN LIVE EVENT/SPECIAL REPORT**  
**AIR DATE:** September 21, 2007 – 16:00 UTC  
**LOCATION:** Beirut, Lebanon  
**ANCHOR:** Wolf Blitzer (The Situation Room, Washington)  
**CORRESPONDENT:** Ben Wedeman (Beirut)

---

**[CNN BREAKING NEWS GRAPHIC: MOURNING IN BEIRUT – MP ANTOINE GHANEM LAID TO REST]**

**WOLF BLITZER, CNN ANCHOR:** You’re watching CNN. I’m Wolf Blitzer reporting from Washington. 

We are following breaking developments out of the Middle East, where tens of thousands of mourners have flooded the streets of Beirut today for the funeral procession of assassinated Lebanese lawmaker Antoine Ghanem. 

Ghanem, an anti-Syrian Christian Member of Parliament from the Kataeb Party, was killed Wednesday in a powerful car bombing in a Christian suburb of Beirut. His death marks the eighth prominent anti-Damascus figure to be assassinated in Lebanon since 2005, and it comes at a profoundly dangerous time for the country—just days before Lebanon’s parliament is scheduled to vote on a new president.

Tensions are running dangerously high, with many in the ruling pro-Western coalition pointing the finger directly at Damascus. Syria has denied any involvement.

CNN’s Senior International Correspondent Ben Wedeman is live on the ground in Beirut following the procession. Ben, describe the atmosphere there today.

---

**BEN WEDEMAN, CNN SENIOR INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT:** Wolf, the atmosphere here in Beirut is a volatile mixture of profound grief and boiling rage. 

Just moments ago, the casket carrying Antoine Ghanem, draped in the red-and-white Lebanese flag and the green cedar emblem of his Kataeb Party, was borne through the streets toward the Sacred Heart Church in Hazmieh. Thousands of mourners lined the route, throwing rice and flowers onto the hearse, while young men chanted anti-Syrian slogans. Many held pictures of Ghanem alongside portraits of former Prime Minister Rafic Hariri, whose 2005 assassination plunged this country into political turmoil.

**(SCENES OF MOURNERS WEEPING, HEAVY MILITARY PRESENCE IN STREETS)**

The security presence here is massive. Armed Lebanese troops and armored personnel carriers are deployed at nearly every major intersection. The government has declared a national day of mourning, shutting down schools, banks, and public institutions.

This isn’t just a funeral, Wolf. It’s a political rally with immense stakes. Ghanem’s death deprives the pro-Western majority of yet another crucial vote in parliament ahead of next week’s presidential election. Leaders of the ruling March 14 coalition say this assassination was a calculated hit designed to derail that vote and destroy Lebanon's fragile democracy.

---

**BLITZER:** Ben, this assassination has drawn fierce condemnation from world leaders, including very strong words coming out of the White House and the United Nations today.

**WEDEMAN:** That’s right, Wolf. The international backlash has been swift and unanimous. Speaking from Washington earlier today, U.S. President George W. Bush strongly condemned the attack, placing the responsibility on regional forces attempting to subvert Lebanese independence.

**PRESIDENT GEORGE W. BUSH [ARCHIVAL AUDIO/QUOTE]:** 
> *"There has been an unthinkable pattern of assassinations targeted at those who are working for a free and democratic Lebanon. The murder of MP Antoine Ghanem is a vicious attempt by regimes in Damascus and Tehran to undermine Lebanon’s sovereignty. The United States stands firmly with the people of Lebanon in their struggle for freedom, and those responsible for these continuous acts of terror must be held accountable."*

**WEDEMAN:** U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, currently attending diplomatic meetings in Europe, echoed those sentiments, calling the bombing a direct assault on the constitutional process in Beirut.

**SECRETARY CONDOLEEZZA RICE [ARCHIVAL AUDIO/QUOTE]:** 
> *"This was a cowardly act of intimidation intended to disrupt the democratic process just as Lebanon prepares to choose its next president. Foreign powers—specifically Syria—must stop their interference in Lebanon’s internal affairs. The international community will not stand by and allow Lebanon’s constitutional framework to be dismantled by political murder."*

**WEDEMAN:** Meanwhile, at UN Headquarters in New York, Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon expressed grave concern over the potential for the country to slide back into civil conflict, reiterating the UN's commitment to establishing a tribunal to investigate these political killings.

**UN SECRETARY-GENERAL BAN KI-MOON [ARCHIVAL AUDIO/QUOTE]:** 
> *"I condemn in the strongest possible terms the terrible assassination of Parliamentarian Antoine Ghanem. This act is an outrage aimed directly at disrupting the democratic process and the upcoming parliamentary elections. I urge all parties in Lebanon to exercise restraint and resolve their political differences through peaceful dialogue."*

---

**WEDEMAN:** But here on the streets of Beirut, Wolf, calls for restraint are falling on deaf ears. Lebanese political leaders from the anti-Syrian bloc gave fiery eulogies today. Former President Amin Gemayel, who lost his own son, Pierre Gemayel, to an assassin’s bullet just ten months ago, warned that the Lebanese people will not be intimidated into submission.

The fear now is what happens next. Parliament is set to convene on September 25th to elect a successor to President Emile Lahoud. With the parliamentary majority now narrowed even further by this assassination, lawmakers are terrified about who might be targeted next. Some MPs have taken refuge in heavily guarded hotels, effectively living in self-imposed exile inside their own country just to survive until the vote.

Beirut is on edge today, Wolf. The funeral may end shortly, but the political crisis in Lebanon is rapidly approaching a dangerous boiling point.

---

**BLITZER:** Ben Wedeman reporting live from Beirut. Ben, thank you for that comprehensive report.

When we return, we’ll analyze what this latest assassination means for the future of the Middle East, and we’ll talk live with a panel of regional experts. 

You’re watching CNN, the worldwide leader in news. Stay with us.

**Shadows Over the Cedar: Antoine Ghanem’s Assassination and the Battle for Lebanon’s Sovereignty**

In September 2007, the fragile tranquility of Beirut was violently shattered once again. A powerful car bomb exploded in the eastern suburb of Sin el-Fil, killing Antoine Ghanem, a prominent Member of Parliament representing the Christian Kataeb (Phalange) Party. Ghanem, a staunchly anti-Syrian politician, became the eighth high-profile pro-sovereignty figure—and the sixth parliamentarian—assassinated in Lebanon since the murder of former Prime Minister Rafic Hariri in February 2005. 

Ghanem’s death was not merely another tragic chapter in Lebanon’s long history of political violence; it was a targeted strike timed precisely to derail an upcoming presidential election. Coming just five days before Parliament was scheduled to convene to select a successor to pro-Syrian President Emile Lahoud, the assassination plunged Lebanon into one of its most severe constitutional and security crises since the end of the 1975–1990 civil war.

---

### A Heartbroken Heartland: The Funeral in Ashrafieh

Days after the blast, the grief and fury of Lebanon’s Christian community culminated in the streets of Ashrafieh, the historic Maronite heartland of Beirut. Tens of thousands of mourners gathered at the Church of the Sacred Heart to bid farewell to the 64-year-old lawmaker and lawyer. 

The atmosphere in Ashrafieh was charged with grief, defiance, and intense political tension. White coffins carrying Ghanem and his two bodyguards were draped in the Lebanese flag and the distinct white-and-green flag of the Kataeb Party, featuring its iconic cedar tree. Streets were lined with black banners and portraits of Ghanem alongside previous martyrs of the "Independence Intifada"—including Pierre Gemayel, the young Kataeb minister assassinated less than a year prior, and journalist Gebran Tueni.

Security was at a maximum. Armed soldiers and police officers cordoned off the district, while armed Kataeb youth stood guard along the procession routes. As the funeral cortege moved through the narrow streets, rice and flower petals were showered from balconies, accompanied by rhythmic clapping and emotional chants demanding the end of foreign interference in Lebanese affairs.

Inside the church, prominent political leaders of the ruling March 14 coalition—a broad alliance of anti-Syrian Sunni, Christian, and Druze factions—sat side by side. Former President Amine Gemayel, leader of the Kataeb Party, delivered a scathing eulogy. He directly accused Damascus and its local proxies of attempting to decapitate Lebanon’s democratic institutions through physical liquidation. "They want to kill our democracy, but we will not surrender," Gemayel declared to a weeping, angry crowd, capturing the existential dread felt by the nation's Christian population.

---

### The Resilience and Target of the Phalange Party

The assassination of Antoine Ghanem cast a glaring spotlight on the Kataeb (Phalange) Party, historically one of the primary political engines of Lebanon’s Maronite Christian establishment. Founded in the 1930s by Pierre Gemayel Sr., the party had long positioned itself as the uncompromising guardian of Lebanese sovereignty and Christian presence in the Middle East.

By 2007, the Kataeb party was paying a disproportionately heavy price in blood for its opposition to Syrian hegemony. The murder of Ghanem was viewed by party faithful not as an isolated incident, but as a deliberate campaign to decimate the leadership of the Kataeb and intimidate the Christian electorate. 

Ghanem himself was a low-key, intellectual politician—a constitutional law expert who had recently returned to Lebanon from self-imposed exile in the United Arab Emirates, where he had fled out of fear for his life. His decision to return was motivated solely by his parliamentary duty: to vote for a sovereign, independent president.

For the Phalange, Ghanem’s death reinforced a narrative of martyrdom. Instead of driving the party into submission, the assassination galvanized its base. It forced the Kataeb to double down on its alliance with Sunni leader Saad Hariri and Druze leader Walid Jumblatt, framing the struggle as a choice between a sovereign democratic state or domination by the "Axis of Resistance" led by Syria and Iran.

---

### The Numbers Game: Impact on the Presidential Vote

To understand the political shockwave caused by Ghanem's murder, one must look at the brutal arithmetic of Lebanon’s Parliament at the time.

The constitution required a supermajority (two-thirds, or 86 out of 128 MPs) to establish a quorum for the first round of a presidential vote. The anti-Syrian March 14 majority held a slim parliamentary advantage over the March 8 opposition, led by Hezbollah, Amal, and Michel Aoun’s Free Patriotic Movement. 

March 14 feared that the opposition would boycott the session to prevent a two-thirds quorum, effectively vetoing any candidate not approved by Damascus and Tehran. In response, March 14 threatened to use their simple majority (half plus one) to elect a president if no consensus was reached. 

This is where the political calculus of assassination became starkly visible:
1. **Chipping Away the Majority:** With every anti-Syrian MP murdered, the March 14 majority shrank. Ghanem’s death reduced the governing coalition’s voting block to 68 seats. 
2. **Atmosphere of Terror:** The message to remaining MPs was terrifyingly clear: showing up to vote could cost them their lives. Several March 14 lawmakers were forced to live in self-imposed exile or hide inside the heavily fortified Phoenicia Hotel in Beirut under 24-hour military guard.
3. **Institutional Paralysis:** By physically reducing the number of anti-Syrian MPs, the assassination narrowed the legal options available to March 14, effectively forcing them to abandon their threat of electing a president by a simple majority without opposition consent.

---

### Geopolitical Fallout and the Path to Vacuum

The murder of Antoine Ghanem drew immediate international condemnation. The UN Security Council, the United States, France, and the Arab League issued fierce statements warning against attempts to destabilize Lebanon's constitutional process. Washington directly pointed the finger at Syria, which denied involvement, as it had with all previous assassinations.

However, international sympathy could not break the domestic political deadlock. The immediate impact on the presidential vote was total paralysis. Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri repeatedly postponed the election sessions as the November 23 deadline—the end of President Emile Lahoud’s term—approached without a consensus candidate.

Ghanem’s assassination succeeded in its immediate tactical goal: it rendered a decisive, independent presidential election impossible in late September 2007. Lebanon eventually entered a protracted presidential vacuum when Lahoud’s term expired, leaving the country without a head of state and governed by a contested caretaker cabinet. 

This vacuum and the accompanying political brinkmanship ultimately culminated eight months later in the May 2008 armed clashes in Beirut, when Hezbollah seized control of parts of the capital. Only then, through the Qatar-brokered Doha Agreement, was a compromise president—Army Chief Michel Suleiman—finally elected.

---

### Legacy of a Murder

Antoine Ghanem’s funeral in Ashrafieh remains a poignant symbol of a tumultuous era in modern Lebanese history. It highlighted the terrifying reality of Lebanese politics in the post-Hariri era, where bullet and bomb were used to alter parliamentary majorities and dictate constitutional outcomes. 

For the Kataeb Party and the wider March 14 movement, Ghanem’s murder was a painful reminder of the cost of defiance. For Lebanon as a nation, the smoke rising from the crater in Sin el-Fil signaled the temporary death of normal democratic governance, proving that in the shadow of regional rivalries, a politician’s vote could be silenced permanently by a lethal political machine.

On the afternoon of September 19, 2007, a powerful car bomb tore through the eastern Beirut suburb of Sin el-Fil. The target was Antoine Ghanem, a 64-year-old Lebanese Member of Parliament and a prominent figure in the Christian Kataeb (Phalange) Party. The blast was so severe that it incinerated several vehicles, shattered nearby buildings, killed at least seven people—including Ghanem and two of his bodyguards—and wounded more than 60 others. 

Ghanem’s assassination was not an isolated act of violence; it was part of a terrifying pattern of targeted killings that had gripped Lebanon since the 2005 assassination of former Prime Minister Rafic Hariri. Ghanem was the eighth anti-Syrian political figure to be murdered in under three years. 

What made Ghanem’s death particularly critical was its timing. Lebanon was embroiled in a severe constitutional crisis, facing a high-stakes parliamentary vote to elect a new president to succeed the pro-Syrian Emile Lahoud. Ghanem was a member of the anti-Syrian March 14 majority coalition. Because the coalition held only a slender majority in Parliament, every vote was vital. Ghanem had actually spent months in self-imposed exile in Europe for his own safety, returning to Beirut just days before the scheduled election to cast his vote. His murder effectively reduced the March 14 coalition's voting block, fueling widespread belief that the assassination was a deliberate attempt to sabotage the democratic process and deny the majority its quorum.

The assassination sparked immediate, fiery condemnation from the international community, which viewed the attack as a direct assault on Lebanon’s fragile democracy and sovereignty.

### The International Reaction

**The United States**
The Bush administration strongly condemned the attack, framing it as part of an ongoing campaign of intimidation by foreign actors—specifically Syria and Iran—to subvert Lebanese independence. 

President George W. Bush issued a blunt statement from Washington, calling the bombing an "act of terrorism" designed to undermine the upcoming presidential election. Bush noted a clear pattern in the targeted killings of anti-Syrian politicians, stating: *"There has been an exercise in intimidation against those who wish to see a free, independent Lebanon... The United States strongly supports the government of Prime Minister Siniora and the forces of democracy in Lebanon."*

**France**
As Lebanon’s historical ally, France reacted with intense outrage. French President Nicolas Sarkozy, who had been actively engaging in diplomatic efforts to resolve the Lebanese political deadlock, expressed deep indignation. 

Sarkozy called the assassination an "odious act" and telephoned Lebanese Prime Minister Fouad Siniora to offer France's total solidarity. French Foreign Minister Bernard Kouchner called for an immediate international investigation and urged the Lebanese people to remain united against attempts to derail their political process, emphasizing that "terror must not be allowed to dictate the political calendar of Lebanon."

**The United Nations**
UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon condemned the attack "in the strongest terms," describing it as a brazen attempt to destabilize Lebanon at a crucial juncture in its political history. Ban reaffirmed the UN’s commitment to supporting the Lebanese government’s sovereignty and stability.

The UN Security Council held an emergency meeting following the blast and issued a formal statement condemning the murder. The Council reiterated its call for an end to political violence in Lebanon and demanded that the perpetrator be held accountable, referencing the ongoing work of the International Independent Investigation Commission (which later led to the creation of the Special Tribunal for Lebanon).

**Regional Dynamics and Syria**
Within Lebanon, leaders of the March 14 alliance explicitly blamed the Syrian regime of Bashar al-Assad for the attack, accusing Damascus of using assassinations to maintain its grip on Lebanese politics despite the withdrawal of Syrian troops in 2005.

The Syrian government, however, swiftly denied any involvement. Syria’s official news agency, SANA, released a brief statement calling the blast a "criminal act" aimed at destroying efforts by Lebanese factions to reach a political compromise. 

The Arab League, led by Secretary-General Amr Moussa, voiced deep concern, warning that the continuous targeting of Lebanese lawmakers threatened to plunge the country back into civil conflict and calling for immediate calm among competing political factions.

### Legacy and Aftermath

Antoine Ghanem’s murder further paralyzed Lebanese politics. The presidential election was postponed multiple times as security fears escalated, forcing many lawmakers to seek refuge inside the fortified Phoenicia Hotel in Beirut until a political compromise was eventually reached months later in Doha, Qatar.

Today, the 2007 bombing remains a grim chapter in Lebanon's turbulent modern history. It stands as a reminder of the dangerous intersection between regional geopolitical rivalries and domestic politics, and highlights a period when international leaders were forced to continually rally behind a Lebanese political system under siege by violence.
